title: Session 21: Multiple Regression
text:
In the previous session, we modeled relationships between two variables by using one variable to predict another. In many real world situations however, outcomes depend on several variables at the same time. For example, engagement during the R training discussion sessions might depend on both preparation and sleep. Multiple regression extends the ideas from linear regression to situations where we use several variables together to make predictions. Importantly, the core ideas remain the same. We still make predictions, calculate residuals, and search for the coefficients that minimize prediction error. The main difference is that we now use more than one predictor variable at a time.
Last time, we searched through many possible lines to find the combination of coefficients that minimized the residual error. As we mentioned then, this is not a very efficient way to fit a regression model, but it gives us an intuitive understanding of what the model is actually doing. In this session, we will use a similar approach. The difference is that instead of searching for the best line, we will search for the best plane.
We will now introduce a simulated dataset that we will use in the first part of this session. The data contains an outcome variable y and two predictor variables x1 and x2. You can download the dataset using the button below and load it into R so that we can begin exploring how adding a second predictor changes our model.


 Download df_1 as csv




Once you have loaded the dataset, begin by exploring the relationships between y, x1, and x2. To do this, use the GGally package (which extends ggplot2 by adding functions that simplify combining geoms with transformed data) and create a pairwise plot using ggpairs() (a function that produces a matrix of plots showing all pairwise relationships between variables). Take a moment to look at how each variable relates to the others, and note any patterns that stand out.

In the previous session, our predictions were based on a line defined by an intercept and a slope. In multiple regression, predictions are instead based on a plane (when working with two predictor variables). Rather than using one predictor variable to make predictions, we now combine information from both x1 and x2.
Our predictions now take the following form:
\[
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x1 + b_2 x2
\]
Here, \(b_0\) represents the intercept, while \(b_1\) and \(b_2\) determine how strongly x1 and x2 influence the predicted values of y.
Before we systematically search for the best combination of coefficients, it is helpful to build some intuition for what the model is doing. Each choice of coefficients defines a different plane in three dimensional space. These planes represent different ways of describing how x1 and x2 relate to y. To get a better sense of this, you will now explore how changing the coefficients changes the plane and how well it fits the data.

In the interactive code chunk below, replace the zeros with values that make the plane fit the data points as closely as possible. You can click and drag on the plot to rotate it and explore the relationships between y, x1, and x2. Finding a good combination of coefficients will likely require some trial and error, but use the patterns you observed in the ggpairs() visualization to guide your guesses.




























When we talked about linear regression with one predictor, we used predictions to compute residuals and then summarized model fit using the residual sum of squares (RSS). We will now apply the same idea in the context of multiple regression. The overall strategy remains unchanged: use the model to make predictions, calculate residuals from those predictions, and then summarize the residuals into a single measure of model fit.

Copy the rss() function from last week and modify it so that it takes two slope coefficients as input. Then use the function to calculate the RSS for your best guesses from exercise 2.

Last week, we used a brute force search to find the coefficient values that minimized the RSS. We can now extend the same idea to multiple regression. Instead of searching across possible values for a single slope coefficient, we now search across combinations of several coefficients simultaneously.
As the number of coefficients increases, a full grid search quickly becomes computationally expensive because the number of coefficient combinations grows very rapidly. Instead of systematically evaluating every possible combination, we will generate many random guesses within a reasonable range of values. While this approach may not identify the exact best coefficients, it will often get us close enough to find a very good fitting model.

There are many ways we could implement a random search procedure. Below, we provide the scaffold for one possible approach using the runif() function, which draws random values from a uniform distribution (meaning that all values within the specified range are equally likely to be selected). Fill in the blanks in the code below. Your work in exercise 2 should help you identify sensible ranges to search within. Then identify the combination of coefficients that produces the smallest RSS.


coef_search <- map(1:10000, \(i) {
  b0 <- runif(n = 1, min = ___, max = ___)
  b1 <- runif(n = 1, min = ___, max = ___)
  b2 <- runif(n = 1, min = ___, max = ___)
  
  df_1 |> 
    rss(_____) |> 
    mutate(b0 = b0, b1 = b1, b2 = b2)
}) |> 
  list_rbind()

While the random search approach can help us find a reasonably good fitting model, it is still computationally inefficient and does not guarantee that we identify the exact coefficient values that minimize the RSS. In practice, we typically rely on specialized optimization algorithms implemented in functions such as lm(), which can efficiently identify the coefficient values that minimize the RSS.

Fit the multiple regression model using lm(). Compare the coefficients produced by lm() to the best values you found through your random search procedure. Hint: additional predictors can be added to the model formula using +.


Interpret the coefficients in this model, focusing on what each coefficient represents when more than one predictor is included in the model. In particular, consider how this interpretation differs from the case of a single predictor model you have seen in earlier work.

In the session on simple linear regression, many different statistical ideas turned out to be closely connected because the model only involved a single predictor. Correlations, slope coefficients, \(R^2\), and permutation-based significance tests were often telling very similar stories about the same underlying relationship between two variables. In multiple regression, these ideas begin to separate into genuinely different concepts because the model must now account for several predictors simultaneously.
The interpretation of \(R^2\) itself remains unchanged: it still measures the proportion of variation in the outcome variable explained by the model. However, in multiple regression the explained variation now comes from several predictors working together rather than from a single predictor alone.
The r2() function we wrote last week allows us to calculate \(R^2\) for simple linear regression. In that case, the model only included a single predictor. To extend this idea to multiple regression, we now need to update the function so that predictions are based on two predictors instead of one. The logic for calculating \(R^2\) remains exactly the same: we compare the variation explained by the model to the total variation in the outcome.

Modify the r2() function so that it works for a multiple regression model with two predictors. In particular, update the prediction step so that it includes both x1 and x2. Then complete the remaining parts of the function so that \(R^2\) is calculated correctly. Call the new function r2_multi.


Use the appropriate r2*() function to compute \(R^2\) for:

A model with x1 as the only predictor (simple regression version)
A model with x2 as the only predictor (simple regression again)
A model with both x1 and x2 as predictors (multiple regression)

Compare the results. Does the model with both predictors explain substantially more variation than the models with only one predictor? How does the combined \(R^2\) compare to the individual \(R^2\) values in this case?







Note



In multiple regression, adding additional predictors will never decrease \(R^2\), even if the new predictors contain very little meaningful information. Because of this, statisticians often use related measures such as adjusted \(R^2\), which penalize models for unnecessary complexity by adjusting for the ratio between the number of observations and the number of predictors in the model. Unlike ordinary \(R^2\), adjusted \(R^2\) can therefore decrease when additional predictors fail to improve the model sufficiently. We will not focus on adjusted \(R^2\) here, but it is important to keep in mind that larger models do not automatically represent better models.


Last week, we used simulation and resampling approaches to assess whether the relationship between a predictor and an outcome variable appeared stronger than we would expect by chance. We will not repeat those ideas in detail here. Instead, we will extend the same logic to a new question that arises in multiple regression: Does adding another predictor meaningfully improve the model fit? We can investigate this by comparing a simpler model containing only x1 to a larger model containing both x1 and x2.
To assess whether the additional explanatory power of x2 is larger than we would expect by chance, we begin by fitting the simpler model containing only x1. The residuals from this model represent the variation in y that remains unexplained after accounting for x1. If x2 does not contain meaningful additional information, then randomly reassigning these residuals should not systematically improve the fit of the larger model. This type of procedure, often called residual permutation, constructs a null distribution for the improvement in model fit by repeatedly permuting the residuals and recalculating the difference in explained variance between the two models. The resulting distribution represents the kinds of improvements in fit (\(\Delta R^2\)) we would expect to observe by chance alone. The observed value of \(\Delta R^2\) from the original data can then be compared to this null distribution to assess whether the improvement in model fit is larger than we would expect by chance.

Complete the code below to generate one permuted dataset under the assumption that x2 does not provide meaningful additional explanatory power beyond x1. The code (if written correctly) should:

Fit a smaller model with only x1 as the predictor
Extract predictions and residuals from this smaller model (here relying on the base R functions predict() and residuals())
Randomly permute (shuffle) the residuals
Create a new outcome variable by adding the permuted residuals back onto the original predictions
Fit both a smaller and a larger model to the permuted data so that we can compare how much additional variation is explained when x2 is added to the model.
Finally calculate how much more variation is explained when x2 is added to the model.



small_mod <- lm(y ~ x1, data = df_1)

df_perm <- df_1 |>
  mutate(pred = predict(_____),
         resid = residuals(_____),
         resid_perm = sample(_____),
         y_perm = _____ + _____)

mod_small <- lm(y_perm ~ x1, data = _____)
mod_large <- lm(y_perm ~ x1 + x2, data = _____)

r2_small <- broom::glance(_____) |> pull(r.squared)
r2_large <- broom::glance(_____) |> pull(r.squared)

tibble(delta_r2 = _____ - _____)


Extend the code from above to repeat the residual permutation procedure 10,000 times. For each iteration, compute the change in explained variance when adding x2 to the model (\(\Delta R^2\)), and store these values to form a null distribution. Next, visualize the null distribution of \(\Delta R^2\) and add the observed \(\Delta R^2\) from the original (non-permuted) data to the plot. Finally, compute a permutation-based p-value, representing the proportion of permuted datasets in which the improvement in model fit (\(\Delta R^2\)) is at least as large as the improvement observed in the real data.
Compare your residual permutation results to the output from lm() + broom::tidy(). Which p-value in this output corresponds to the one you just calculated using residual permutation?

We will now apply the same workflow to new datasets generated under different conditions. Although the computational steps remain the same, the interpretation of the results changes substantially depending on the relationships between the predictors and the outcome variable. Download the new data linked below.




 Download df_2 as csv





 Download df_3 as csv






Apply the analysis workflow developed in this session to df_2 and df_3. Begin by visualizing the relationships between the variables before fitting both a smaller model (y ~ x1) and a larger model (y ~ x1 + x2). Then calculate and compare the corresponding \(R^2\) values, compute the observed \(\Delta R^2\), and use residual permutation to generate a null distribution for \(\Delta R^2\). Visualize each null distribution together with the observed \(\Delta R^2\), and calculate a permutation-based p-value assessing whether adding x2 meaningfully improves the model fit. After completing the analyses, compare the results across the two datasets and reflect on how differences in the relationships between the predictors influence the interpretation of the models and the permutation-based inference results.


As a final step, use lm() to fit separate simple regression models for each predictor individually (for example, y ~ x1 and y ~ x2) and examine their \(R^2\) values and model summaries using broom::glance() and broom::tidy(). Compare these results to the permutation-based inference results from the multiple regression models. In particular, consider whether predictors that appear important in isolation also provide substantial additional explanatory power once other predictors are already included in the model.

So far, we have assumed that the relationship between a predictor and the outcome is constant across all observations. We now relax this assumption by allowing the effect of x1 to differ between two groups defined by a binary variable (group, coded 0/1). This is an example of an interaction, where the effect of one variable depends on the value of another.

You will now explore two new datasets that both contain y, x1, and group. Download these data by clicking the buttons below.





 Download df_4 as csv





 Download df_5 as csv






For both df_4 and df_5, begin by visualizing (using regular ggplot()) the relationship between x1 and y, coloring or grouping points by group, and adding simple trend lines for each group. Pay attention to whether the relationship between x1 and y appears similar or different across the two groups.
Next, fit two models (using lm()) to each dataset: an additive model (y ~ x1 + group) and an interaction model (y ~ x1 * group). Use broom::tidy() to inspect and compare the estimated coefficients from the two models (note that the interaction term is the one including a :), and broom::glance() to compare overall model fit statistics (including \(R^2\)). In particular, examine whether allowing the effect of x1 to vary by group leads to a noticeable improvement in model fit.
Relate the model results back to the patterns you observed in the plots. Focus especially on how the relationship between x1 and y changes (or does not change) across groups, and how this is reflected in the presence or absence of an interaction effect.

title: Session 19: Project work II
text:
After another five weeks of training, it is time to return to your own project data. In this part of the course, you will practice applying the methods we have covered so far, with particular focus on more recent topics such as ANOVA, chi-square tests, and multiple comparisons correction.
Although this session is based on your own project data, the exercises will also involve manipulating and restructuring variables, as well as some simulation. This is done to ensure that the statistical concepts we study can be clearly illustrated in a controlled way, since real datasets do not always naturally contain the structure needed to demonstrate these ideas.
By next Wednesday, you should be prepared to present your work, together with a report that includes figures and your main statistical conclusions. Your report should clearly show what you did, what you found, and how you interpret your results. Organize your work in Quarto, combining code, results, and reflections into a single self-contained document.

In your own dataset, identify two variables that you will use for the following analyses. One of these variables must be categorical; choose a variable with multiple distinct categories, ideally as many as your data reasonably allow. The second variable, which will serve as the outcome, can be either numeric or categorical.


Create a visualization that shows the relationship between the two variables you selected. Choose a plot type that is appropriate for the types of variables you are working with.
Run an omnibus test (ANOVA or chi-square) to assess the overall relationship between the two variables, taking into account repeated observations if relevant. Calculate an appropriate measure of effect size. Use a resampling technique (bootstrapping or permutation) to estimate the statistical significance.
Irrespective of the outcome of the omnibus test, perform follow-up post hoc tests (e.g., pairwise comparisons of means or analysis of standardized residuals). Create a table that includes the uncorrected p-values as well as p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using two approaches: one that adjusts each comparison separately (for example Bonferroni or FDR), and one that directly accounts for multiple testing through permutation.
Finally, extend your earlier visualization to summarize the post hoc results. Add information about the pairwise comparisons to the plot, indicating significance using both uncorrected and adjusted p-values. The plot should clearly show how the interpretation of the results changes depending on whether multiple comparisons are accounted for.


In this exercise, you will analyze the relationship between two variables in your dataset using several different approaches. The goal is to compare how different ways of representing the same data affect the results you obtain.


Start by selecting two continuous variables from your dataset. These can be the same two numeric variables you analysed for exercise 3 in the Project work 1 session, or different ones if you so prefer. We will refer to these variables as x and y. Compute the correlation between x and y, and assess its significance using a permutation test. Record the correlation coefficient and the p-value, and briefly describe what you conclude from this analysis.
Next, mutate a new version of x by dividing it into 6 groups of roughly equal size, for example using the ntile() function as described here. Now use this grouped version of x to run a one-way ANOVA with y as the outcome, by calculating the F-statistic and using permutation to compute the p-value. Record the results and the group means.
Then, create a second version of x in which it is divided into only 3 groups. As above, run a one-way ANOVA with y as the outcome and record the results.
Now compare the results from the analyses you have just performed. How does the statistical significance differ across the different versions of x? Do the conclusions you would draw about the relationship between x and y change depending on how x is represented? Before continuing, briefly note whether you expected these differences, and why.
In the next step, create a categorical version of y by dividing it into two groups representing values above and below the median. Using this categorical version of y together with your three-group version of x, perform a chi-square test of independence, again relying on permutation to calculate the p-value. Record the results and compare them to your earlier analyses. To what extent do the different approaches lead to similar or different conclusions?
Finally, we want you to investigate whether the patterns you observed are specific to your dataset or reflect a more general phenomenon. Using your data as a reference, the task is to simulate data where the population correlation matches the correlation you observed at the start of this exercise. Since we have not previously simulated data with a given correlation, we provide some starter code to guide you. In the code chunk below, we use the mvrnorm() function from the MASS package to draw two variables from a multivariate normal distribution. Here, “multivariate” means that, in addition to specifying the means and variances, we can also control the covariance between the sampled variables by supplying a variance–covariance matrix (Sigma =) as input. In the example code below we set the variance to 1 (the diagonal in the sigma matrix) so that any value specified for r represents the correlation.


library(MASS)

r <- 0.3
sigma <- matrix(c(1, r, r, 1), nrow = 2)

df <- mvrnorm(n = 100, mu = c(1, 1), Sigma = sigma) |> 
  as_tibble()


Now use methods you have learned throughout the course to write code that generates 10,000 simulated datasets. Each dataset should contain two variables, with a sample size and correlation structure chosen to resemble what you observed in your own data. For each simulated dataset, do the following:

For each simulated dataset, calculate the p-value for the correlation between the two variables. For computational efficiency, use the cor.test() function, and use the tidy() function from the broom package to extract the p-value from the output.
For each simulated dataset, create grouped versions of one of the variables (referred to as x above) using the ntile() function to form approximately equal-sized groups. As before, create one version with six groups and one with three groups. Use the aov() function to perform ANOVAs for each version, and use tidy() to extract and store the corresponding p-values.
Now create a two-group version of the y variable. For each simulated dataset, run a chi-square test using the chisq.test() function to examine the relationship between this two-group version of y and the three-group version of x. Save the resulting p-values using the tidy() function
Study the proportion of significant p-values (i.e., the statistical power) for each of the different representations of the simulated data, and visualize the results. Explain what you observe.



Using the same simulation approach as in the previous exercise, compute appropriate measures of effect size corresponding to each analysis (for example correlation, eta-squared, or Cramer’s V, depending on the representation). To do this, modify the code you have already written so that it also returns effect size estimates in addition to p-values. In other words, keep the same simulation structure, but extend the output so that each simulated dataset includes both the p-value and the corresponding effect size measure for each analysis.







Note



Although these effect size measures are defined on different scales, they can be considered comparable enough for the purpose of examining overall patterns in the simulations. In particular, since most are bounded between 0 and 1, and correlations can be interpreted in terms of absolute strength, we will focus on how they behave rather than on exact numerical equivalence.



Examine how the distribution of effect sizes differs across representations, and visualize these distributions to better understand how effect size estimates vary depending on how the data are represented. Compare these patterns to the results you obtained for statistical power in the previous exercise.
As an additional step, examine how effect sizes behave when focusing only on statistically significant results across simulations. Compare these selected effect sizes to the overall distribution of effect sizes across all simulations. Visualize this by highlighting or coloring the effect sizes corresponding to significant results within the same distribution plot. Reflect on how restricting attention to significant results influences the estimated magnitude of effects.

title: Session 20: Linear Regression
text:
This week we will learn about linear regression. In keeping with the style from the early days of the statistics training, we will start by watching what Josh Starmer has to say about this topic in this StatQuest video (Linear Regression, Clearly Explained!!!).
We introduce some data in the code chunk below.

library(tidyverse)
d1_lm <- tibble(x = 1:10,
                y = c(0.56, 2.99, 3.16, 4.18, 2.64, 
                      5.39, 2.37, 5.52, 6.57, 5.71))

Using the values in d1_lm, we will learn how to find the best-fitting line and what statistical conclusions we can draw about it once it is identified. But before we get to that, let’s take a look at these data in a scatterplot.

d1_lm |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  theme_linedraw(base_size = 14) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








We see a rather clear linear relationship between x and y. Recall that the equation for a linear regression line (one predictor) is:
\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\] Where:

\(\hat{y}\) = predicted value of the outcome
\(x\) = predictor variable
\(\beta_0\) = intercept (value of \(\hat{y}\) when \(x = 0\)
\(\beta_1\) = slope (change in \(\hat{y}\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\))


Study the plot above, imagine a line representing the relationship between x and y and see if you can guess the approximate values for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).

The first thing we are going to do in order to later find the best-fitting line, is to write a function that lets us add predicted values (\(\hat{y}\)) to any tibble. This function will take the data as well as \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) as inputs and add a column with predicted values to the data.

Fill in the blanks in the function below so that the predicted values are calculated correctly for a given \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).


add_preds <- function(data, x_col, intercept, slope){
  data |> 
    mutate(pred = _____ + _____ * {{_____}})
}


Next, use this function to help you recreate the plot below, adding the trend line using geom_line(). This time, make sure you combine the data and use facet_wrap() to create the individual panels, rather than relying on functions for the patchwork package.










We hope you will agree that, out of these four sets of guesses for the intercept and slope, the pair \(\beta_0 = 1\) and \(\beta_1 = 0.5\) appears to produce the best-fitting line. Why? One quick way to assess the fit is to look at how many points fall on each side of the line. The more evenly the points are split, the better the fit tends to be. However, a far better approach is to study the residuals, which represent the distances between the observed values and the predicted values from the line. Examining the residuals provides a more systematic and precise way to evaluate how well a line fits the data, allowing us to quantify the error rather than just eyeballing the pattern. Below we show code how vertical lines representing the residuals can be added to the \(\beta_0 = 1\) and \(\beta_1 = 0.5\) plot.

d1_lm |> 
  add_preds(x, 1, 0.5) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x, xend = x,
                   y = pred, yend = y),
               color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y),
             size = 3) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x, 
                y = pred), 
            color = "blue") +
  labs(y = "y") +
  theme_linedraw(base_size = 14) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  annotate("curve",
           x = 7.85,  y = 2.85,
           xend = 7.2, yend = 3.2, 
           curvature = 0.45,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.17, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", label = "Residual",
           x = 7.75, y = 2.62, size = 4, 
           hjust = 0)








In plain words, residuals show how wrong the line is at each point. We can therefore define the best-fitting line as the one that minimizes the distances between the observed values and the predicted values. If we square these distances and sum them we get the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS):
\[RSS = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
The goal of linear regression is to find values of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that that minimize the RSS. This is known as the least squares principle, and it is the reason why the most common form of linear regression is called least squares regression.

Let’s test this idea to see how the four intercept/slope guesses we presented above translates into RSS values. Fill in the blanks below so that RSS is outputted for each intercept/slope pair. Reflect on how the RSS values correspond to the plots from the previous exercise.


d1_lm |> 
  add_preds(___, ___, ___) |> 
  mutate(guess = "intercept = 1, slope = 1") |> 
  add_row(d1_lm |> 
            add_preds(___, ___, ___) |> 
            mutate(guess = "intercept = 1, slope = 0.5")) |> 
  add_row(d1_lm |> 
            add_preds(___, ___, ___) |> 
            mutate(guess = "intercept = 0, slope = 1")) |> 
  add_row(d1_lm |> 
            add_preds(___, ___, ___) |> 
            mutate(guess = "intercept = 0, slope = 0.5")) |> 
  group_by(_____) |> 
  mutate(resid = y - _____) |> 
  summarize(rss = _____)

The probability that we found the best intercept/slope combination by guessing only four times is very low. Instead, we are now going to perform a so-called grid search: we will test many values that differ by small increments, try them all, and identify the combination that produces the smallest RSS.

The first thing we need, to make iterating across many intercepts and slopes easier, is a function that takes any tibble together with a chosen intercept and slope, calculates the RSS, and returns it. Fill in the blanks to complete the function below.


rss <- function(data, x_col, y_col, intercept, slope){
  data |> 
    mutate(pred = _____ + _____ * {{_____}},
           resid = {{_____}} - _____) |> 
    summarize(rss = _____)
}

Next, we generate our guesses. We saw above that the best intercept appears to be somewhere around 1, so we will “search” in that vicinity. We do the same for the slope, focusing on values around 0.5. We begin by placing our sequences in a tibble and then use the expand() function to create all combinations of intercept and slope values. We then use the map2() function, which allows us to iterate over two sequences simultaneously. Finally, we add our newly calculated RSS values to the guesses tibble so that we can keep track of which RSS value belongs to each intercept/slope pair.

Complete the code below so that the intercept sequence in the guesses tibble ranges from 0.75 to 1.25 in steps of 0.001. Do the same for the slope values, but this time let the range be from 0.25 to 0.75.


guesses <- tibble(intercept = seq(____, ____, ____),
                  slope = seq(____, ____, ____)) |> 
  expand(intercept, slope)

rsss <- map2(guesses |> pull(intercept), 
             guesses |> pull(slope),
             \(i, j) rss(d1_lm, x, y, i, j)) |> 
  list_rbind()

is_rss <- guesses |> 
  add_column(_____)


Now use the is_rss object to find the intercept and slope values corresponding to the best-fitting line. Plot the results and explain how the intercept and slope values should be interpreted.
The map2() call took a while to run. In reality, we do not need to perform a grid search to find the best intercept and slope. The lm() function computes these values for us automatically using a closed-form solution. Instead of trying many combinations, lm() applies the least-squares formulas directly, using linear algebra to calculate the exact coefficients that minimize the RSS. This makes the estimation precise, fast, and mathematically guaranteed to find the optimal line without searching over a grid of possibilities.
Run the code below and check that the lm() algorithm finds the same intercept and slope as the grid search did.


lm(y ~ x, data = d1_lm)



Josh spends quite a bit of time talking about the main effect size measure associated with linear regression: r-squared (\(R^2\)), also known as the coefficient of determination. The formula for calculating \(R^2\) is straightforward:
\[R^2 = \frac{TSS - RSS}{TSS}  \] Where:

TSS (total sum of squares) = \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \bar{y})^2\)
RSS is calculated the same way as before.

The rrs() function we wrote earlier gets us about halfway to calculating \(R^2\). All we need to do now is calculate the total sum of squares and finally find the variance explained by the regression line.

Complete the r2() function by filling in the blanks so that \(R^2\) is calculated correctly.


r2 <- function(data, x_col, y_col, intercept, slope){
  data |> 
    mutate(pred = _____ + _____ * {{_____}},
           resid = {{_____}} - _____, 
           mean_y = mean({{_____}}),
           dev_y = {{_____}} - _____) |> 
    summarize(rss = _____, 
              tss = _____, 
              R2 = (_____ - _____) / _____) |> 
    select(R2)
}


It is, however, a bit tedious to manually input the intercept and slope values in the function above every time you want to calculate \(R^2\). In most situations, we would simply let the lm() function compute \(R^2\) for us. We can use the glance() function from the broom package, which we introduced several weeks ago, to output the values we want in a tidy (easily transformable) format. Run the code below and make sure that you completed the r2() function correctly by comparing the \(R^2\) from that function to the lm() + glance() output.


lm(y ~ x, data = d1_lm) |> 
  broom::glance()


How would you interpret the \(R^2\) in this case. If the effect small or large?
Calculate the correlation coefficient (\(r\)) comparing x and y in the d1_lm data and explain how it compares to \(R^2\).

Josh shows how we can calculate the p-value for the effect size by first computing the F-statistic (as we learned in the ANOVA sessions) and using simulation to generate a null distribution. This is a valid approach and one you can try for yourself, and the results from a theory-based version of this test is given by the glance() function. However, nothing prevents us from using the \(R^2\) value directly and comparing it to a simulated null distribution: by repeatedly generating data under the null hypothesis, calculating \(R^2\) for each simulated dataset, and then seeing where our observed \(R^2\) falls in that distribution, we can estimate a p-value and assess the significance of the effect size without relying on the F-statistic.

Complete the code below to generate a \(R^2\) null distribution. What do you expect the null distribution to look like in this case? Make a prediction about the shape of the distribution, and then check whether your expectation was correct by making a histogram. Show that using simulated \(R^2\) indeed works by computing the p-value and comparing it to the one from the glance() output.


obs_r2 <- lm(___ ~ ___, data = d1_lm) |> 
  broom::glance() |> 
  pull(_____)

sims <- map(1:10000, \(i) tibble(x = 1:10, 
                                 y = rnorm(10)))

rsq <- map(sims, \(i) lm(___ ~ ___, data = i) |> 
             broom::glance()) |> 
  list_rbind()


Would a permutation test based on \(R^2\) have given the same result as the simulation-based approach in this case? Justify your answer by generating a permutation-based null distribution for \(R^2\) and comparing the two approaches numerically and/or graphically.

The p-value we calculated above tells us whether the model as a whole is statistically significant. Specifically, it tests the null hypothesis that the slope coefficient is equal to zero, meaning that there is no linear relationship between the predictor and the response variable. A small p-value indicates that the model provides a better fit than a model with no predictor. The next step is to evaluate the uncertainty and significance of the slope estimate itself.

Next, we want you to do two things: calculate the standard error of the slope estimate using bootstrapping, and calculate the p-value for the slope using permutation. You can reuse code from above and from previous sessions, and check your calculations by comparing the results to the output from the code below, where the term == "x" row represents the slope coefficient.


lm(y ~ x, data = d1_lm) |> 
  broom::tidy()


Compare the p-value for the slope to the p-value obtained from the \(R^2\) -based test above. What do you notice, and why do you think this happens in simple linear regression?







Note



At this stage, simple (one predictor) linear regression can feel surprisingly redundant from a statistical perspective. Several quantities that are introduced as different ideas turn out to be very closely connected when there is only one predictor. For example, the correlation between x and y and the model’s \(R^2\) are mathematically closely related. You may also have noticed that the simulation- and permutation-based significance test for \(R^2\) seems to tell a story very similar to the significance test for the slope coefficient. This is not a coincidence. In simple regression, many of these tools are different ways of looking at essentially the same relationship between two variables. This apparent redundancy will become much more useful next week when we introduce multiple regression. With several predictors, ideas that currently seem almost interchangeable begin to separate into genuinely different concepts.



We will now move from simulated examples to real data using the penguins dataset we have worked with several times before. Using simple linear regression, investigate the relationship between bill length and bill depth in Chinstrap penguins. What is the change in bill depth for a one-unit increase in bill length? Calculate the 95% confidence interval for this estimate. How would you interpret the intercept in this case? What is the effect size?


Investigate whether body mass is predicted by penguin sex using linear regression. How would you interpret the slope coefficient in this case, and what familiar quantity might it correspond to?
